title: Farid: don't strike back
hookLine: if someone hits you, don't hit back; kiss their feet and go home (Farid salok, ang 1378)

cards: A driver cuts across the lane, then leans on the horn as if it were the other person's fault. A relative makes the comment, the one that always comes, in front of everyone.
The comeback is ready: the return honk, the line that'll put them in their place. It lands for a moment. Then it gets carried home and chewed on all night.
Sheikh Farid has a couplet for exactly this moment.

teach.h: JO TAI MAARAN MUKEEAAN — IF STRUCK.
teach.b: On Ang 1378, among Farid's saloks: fareedaa jo tai maaran mukeeaan tinhaa na maare ghumm; aapnarai ghar jaaeeai pair tinhaa de chumm. Farid, those who strike you with their fists, don't turn around and strike them back.

teach.h: KISS THEIR FEET: HUMILITY, NOT REVENGE.
teach.b: Kiss their feet, and go home. Kiss their feet? In the Punjab, touching someone's feet is a sign of respect and humility.
He's asking for the opposite of revenge: meet the blow with humility, then walk away to your own home, your own peace, without carrying the fight with you.
Farid isn't saying the blow was fine, or that wrong doesn't matter. Just before it, he tells the clever to bow their heads and look into their own collar.
Later he says: do good to the one who does you wrong, and don't let anger into the mind. And notice the last line: go home.

teach.h: FOR YOURSELF, LET GO; FOR OTHERS, STAND.
teach.b: Don't stand there and take more. Don't keep the quarrel alive. Four days ago, Kabir praised the hero who fights for the helpless.
So which is it? One reading holds the two together. When the blow is against you, your own pride, your own honor, you can let it go and go home.
When the helpless are being crushed, you stand on the field. The ego doesn't get to fight for itself; the weak get defended.

That's the whole week, in a way: a weaver at his loom, one light in everyone, a warrior for the helpless, a death that delights, Kabir's short sharp saloks, and Farid, the first Punjabi voice, saying go home in peace.

how: Farid's saloks are read in the Guru Granth Sahib and quoted by Sikhs about humility and forgiveness in personal quarrels, alongside the Sikh duty to defend others who are wronged.

o: a Sikh Guru who wrote hymns on forgiveness
the Sufi who said don't strike back, go home
a Hindu saint who taught bowing at the feet

games.q: inside Farid's salok — tap the pairs.

s: Farid says the blow was fine and doesn't matter
he asks for humility instead of revenge, then says go home and leave the fight.
Farid's salok asks for humility instead of revenge
kiss their feet, and go home.
Farid says to stay and take more blows
he says go home: leave the fight where it happened.

games.q: someone strikes you in a quarrel. what does Farid's salok say to do?
o: don't strike back; meet it with humility and go home.
stay and argue until they apologize.
games.why: tinhaa na maare ghumm... aapnarai ghar jaaeeai: don't turn and hit back; kiss their feet, and go home in peace.

practice: Bring to mind one slight you're still carrying, a comment, a snub, a small unfairness from this week, and notice where it sits in your body.
Then picture yourself, as Farid says, bowing slightly to it, turning and walking home; the door closes behind you, and the fight stays outside. Breathe out, and let your shoulders drop.

wordCard.voice: Farid. Here, his salok: if someone strikes you, don't strike back; meet it with humility and go home. This week: Kabir the weaver, one light, the true warrior, the death that delights, saloks, Farid of Pakpattan, and Farid again.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: fareedaa, O Farid, the way his saloks address himself.

carryVoice: Your line: go home in peace. The quarrel can stay where it happened. Another week, walked.
